archetype.name: Pocket Passer (under-center, intermediate-driven)
archetype.definition: A statuesque rhythm thrower who adds no value with his legs and makes his living hitting the 10-to-20-yard window on time, mostly to his tight end, while living with the interceptions that come with that window.

report.headline: A 38-year-old rebound built on Bowers and the intermediate game, now tested.
report.take:
Cousins at 38 is the same quarterback he has been for a decade: no mobility (7 rushing yards on 22 carries, and the two rushing scores are sneaks), quick decisions, and a passing game that lives between the numbers at the second level. What changed is the quality of the throwing. Last year in Atlanta looked like the end of the line: a -2.8 CPOE and 6.4 yards per attempt, both near the bottom of the league. This year he is back to his Minnesota-era shape, with CPOE up 4.2 points, YPA up 1.03 and 0.167 EPA per dropback, 13th of 49. Under Klint Kubiak he is better under center (0.165 EPA) than in shotgun (0.092), which fits a play-action, timing-based offense that suits him.

The value is concentrated. His throws of 10+ air yards add 53.6 EPA. Everything under 10 nets to essentially zero, because the 52 throws behind the line cost 18.6 EPA. Some of that is the screen-and-swing game feeding Ashton Jeanty, whose 56 targets produce almost nothing. Brock Bowers is the engine: 70 targets at 0.531 EPA per target, worth more than every other receiver combined. Third down has been outstanding: 0.411 EPA, 10 touchdowns, no interceptions and a 47.7% conversion rate at an average of 7.2 yards to go. With a run game 30th in EPA and a defense 28th, the Raiders need all of it.

The numbers hide two things. First, the 20 touchdowns (2nd in the league) rest on a 6.3% TD rate and 15 red-zone scores on a 48.1% red-zone completion rate. That is unusually efficient finishing and should cool, and it already has (5.3% over the last five). Second, the interceptions are structural. Five of his eight come on intermediate throws, the same area that produces most of his value, and his career is full of bottom-tier interception ranks (55th of 59 in 2020, 64th of 68 in 2022, 59th of 60 in 2024). That is the cost of how he plays, not a slump.

The recent path depends on the opponent. Against the Rams (4th-ranked defense now) he posted -7.4 EPA, and against the 49ers (7th) he threw three interceptions. Against the Jets (25th) he produced a season-best 16.4. His last three games sit 0.085 EPA per dropback below his season rate, even with CPOE up. Against soft defenses he is a top-12 producer. Against good ones, especially ones that take away the intermediate and deep windows, he becomes a volume passer who turns it over.

strengths.title: Intermediate and deep efficiency
strengths.body: Nearly all of his passing value comes from throws of 10+ air yards: 0.38 EPA on intermediate attempts and 0.71 on deep ones, with a positive CPOE downfield. This is his career skill set, timing and anticipation into the second level, and it rebounded from last year's dip. The deep number rests on 30 attempts and will soften, but the intermediate game is durable.

strengths.title: Bowers as the offense's engine
strengths.body: Bowers has drawn 70 targets at 0.531 EPA per target, which makes him the reason the Raiders' passing offense ranks 10th despite a 30th-ranked run game. Cousins trusts him on the middle-depth throws that drive his value. As long as Bowers is healthy, this connection is the most reliable part of the profile.

strengths.title: Sack avoidance and third-down command
strengths.body: He turns only 15.3% of pressures into sacks, 2nd-best in the league, and his 3.4% sack rate ranks 4th. He gets the ball out rather than hold it, a trait his career shows in most seasons. Third down has been a strength at 0.411 EPA with 10 touchdowns. The zero interceptions on third down will not last, but the conversion rate is backed by real process.

concerns.title: Interceptions are part of the package
concerns.body: His 8 interceptions rank 44th of 49, and 5 came on intermediate throws. That is the same window that makes him productive, and his career shows the same bottom-tier interception ranks year after year. Expect roughly one a game against good coverage. The three against San Francisco is what that looks like.

concerns.title: Good defenses flatten him
concerns.body: His worst games came against the Rams (4th-ranked defense now) and the 49ers (7th), and his last-three EPA per dropback sits well below his season rate. Without mobility or a credible run game behind him, a defense that removes the second-level window leaves him with an underneath game that adds nothing.

concerns.title: Touchdown rate running hot
concerns.body: A 6.3% TD rate and 15 red-zone touchdowns on a 48.1% red-zone completion rate is finishing efficiency that rarely holds across a season. It has already slid to 5.3% over the last five games. Volume stays, but scoring should drift toward the league norm.

trend.note: The game log swings with the opponent: -7.4 EPA against the Rams, a season-best 16.4 against the Jets, then three interceptions in San Francisco. The underlying accuracy (last-three CPOE of 4.2) is fine; the results depend on whether the defense allows the second-level window.

nextGame.headline: Seattle's lid-on-top defense takes away exactly where he lives
nextGame.body:
This is close to the worst stylistic draw for him. Seattle ranks 1st in deep-pass EPA allowed and 1st in explosive pass rate, 4th in pass EPA, and has allowed the fewest quarterback passing yards per game. Cousins' value lives almost entirely on throws of 10+ air yards. The opening Seattle leaves is underneath, where its short-pass EPA allowed ranks only 21st, but his under-10 game has netted nothing all year. Tight ends have barely produced against Seattle (TE1 EPA per play rank 8), so even the Bowers lifeline is contested. The Raiders are 3.5-point home underdogs indoors with a modest 43.5 total, so the shootout volume that has fed him lately is less likely.

Availability cuts both ways. Seattle is missing DT Leonard Williams and LB Uchenna Nwosu, which should dent a pass rush that ranks 4th in hit rate and gives him slightly cleaner pockets to work the intermediate area. Seattle's offense is depleted: Sam Darnold is out, Drew Lock is questionable with an oblique he is expected to play through, and left tackle Charles Cross and guard Quenton Nelson are both out. A run-leaning Seattle team (pass rate 5.9 points under expected) with a backup quarterback and two missing linemen points to a slower, lower-possession game. That keeps Las Vegas within one score, where Cousins is at his best, but it caps his attempts.

keyMatchups.title: Second-level throws versus elite coverage
keyMatchups.body: Seattle allows the least deep-pass EPA in the league and the fewest explosive passes, while 53.6 of Cousins' EPA comes on 10+ yard throws. If Seattle keeps the lid on, he has to live underneath, where his production goes flat.

keyMatchups.title: Bowers against Seattle's tight-end coverage
keyMatchups.body: Bowers is the one receiver who reliably wins in the middle of the field, and Seattle has held lead tight ends to near-neutral EPA per target. Seattle's short-area EPA allowed (21st) is the soft spot, so a heavy diet of quick Bowers targets may be the plan.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted Seattle offense shapes script
keyMatchups.body: With Darnold out and Cross and Nelson sidelined, Seattle's 23rd-ranked offense is unlikely to build a big lead. That keeps the Raiders out of the chase script where Cousins has been less efficient (0.08 EPA when trailing by 9+). The trade-off is fewer possessions in a game totaled at 43.5.

nextGame.watch: Whether he keeps taking intermediate shots into Seattle's coverage or settles for checkdowns. His interception count and his yardage will both follow that choice.

restOfSeason.body:
The rebound looks real. The accuracy and YPA gains put him back in line with his 2019-2021 seasons rather than the 2025 outlier, and the Bowers connection plus a defense that keeps forcing him to throw should keep volume around 35 attempts a game. What should regress is the scoring. The TD rate and red-zone finishing are running well above his usual level, so expect roughly 1.5 to 2 touchdowns a game rather than the 2.22 he has posted. The interceptions will not go away, because they come from the same throws that make him good.

Week to week, sort the schedule by defensive quality. Against bottom-half defenses he is a strong producer. Against top-10 units, especially ones that take away the intermediate and deep windows, the efficiency drops sharply. A floor of real volume and a ceiling dependent on the opponent is the profile.
swingFactors: Whether the 28th-ranked Raiders defense keeps forcing shootouts

confidence.note: Nine starts, and the profile matches his long career; the TD rate and recent swings rest on small, opponent-driven samples.
